title: Interior Decoration Basics
subtitle: Plan and deliver a beautiful, practical room makeover on a real budget, from client brief to finished, photographed result.
description: Learn the principles decorators use (balance, scale, focal point and colour), then the practical skills: measuring and drawing a floor plan, planning lighting, calculating curtain fabric and paint, and budgeting with local materials. You finish by running a client brief, writing a quotation and documenting a real room transformation for your portfolio.
outcomes: Assess a room and explain changes using balance, scale, proportion and focal point
Build colour schemes with the colour wheel and the 60-30-10 guide
Measure a room, draw a 1:50 floor plan and plan layered lighting
Calculate curtain fabric, paint quantities and a makeover budget with contingency
Run a client brief, write an itemised quotation and hand over a finished room safely
Document before and after results in a portfolio that wins clients
audience: Women who want to decorate homes, shops, salons or short-let apartments for clients, or transform their own spaces, with practical skills and modest budgets.
tools: 5 m or 8 m steel tape measure
Graph paper (1 cm squares), pencil, ruler and scissors
Paint colour cards and fabric swatches from local shops

modules.title: Foundations: how decorators see a room
modules.overview: Before buying anything, a good decorator learns to read a room: what it is for, what feels wrong and why. This module covers the decorating process, the core design principles of balance, scale and focal point, and how to choose colours with the colour wheel.

lessons.title: What a decorator does and the 7-stage decorating process
objectives: Explain the difference between interior decoration and interior design
Describe the seven stages of a decorating job from brief to handover
Assess a room by its function, its users and its problems before suggesting changes
Write a short room assessment for a real space

blocks.text: Interior decoration is the work of making a room look good and work well using **colour, furniture arrangement, lighting, fabrics, accessories and finishes**. A decorator works with the room as it is built. An interior designer may also change the structure: moving walls, redesigning a kitchen layout, planning new wiring. In this course you are learning decoration. When a client asks for structural work, plumbing or new electrical points, your job is to bring in a qualified builder, plumber or electrician, not to do it yourself.

blocks.name: interior-design
blocks.alt: A woman arranging furniture and a lamp in a living room
blocks.caption: Decoration works with the room as it is: furniture, colour, light and fabric.

blocks.text: Start with function, not with things

Beginners often start with things they like: a sofa they saw on Instagram, a colour from a friend's house. Professionals start with three questions. **What is this room for?** (sleeping, receiving guests, studying, selling to customers). **Who uses it, and when?** (a family of six in the evening, a grandmother who walks with a stick, children doing homework). **What is not working now?** (too dark, too crowded, too hot, nowhere to put things). Every choice later in this course must answer one of these questions.
The seven stages of a decorating job

blocks.title: From first visit to handover
items: Brief and site visit
Measure and plan
Concept and colours
Budget and quotation
Source and buy
Install and style
Handover and photos
blocks.caption: Every job, big or small, moves through these stages in this order.

items: **Brief and site visit:** listen to the client, see the room, take photos from each corner and note problems.
**Measure and plan:** measure the room, windows, doors and sockets, and draw a simple floor plan (Module 2).
**Concept and colours:** choose a colour scheme, a focal point and a furniture layout, and show them on a simple mood board.
**Budget and quotation:** list every item with its cost, add labour and transport, and agree a written quotation (Module 4).
**Source and buy:** buy fabric, paint and accessories, and book any tradespeople such as painters or electricians.
**Install and style:** paint, hang curtains, arrange furniture, place lighting and accessories.
**Handover and photos:** walk the client through the room, take after photos from the same spots as the before photos, and ask for feedback.

blocks.title: Do not skip the before photos
blocks.text: Before you move a single chair, photograph the room from every corner and the doorway. These photos help you plan, protect you if there is a dispute, and become the 'before' half of your portfolio.
Reading a room: the five-point check

items: **Light:** where do the windows face? Is the room bright in the morning and dark by afternoon? Which bulbs are fitted?
**Flow:** can people walk from the door to the window and seats without squeezing past furniture?
**Clutter and storage:** what is on the floor, on top of cabinets, behind doors? Clutter is often a storage problem, not a style problem.
**Colour and condition:** wall colour, stains, peeling paint, faded curtains, worn upholstery.
**Climate and practical needs:** heat, dust, power cuts, mosquitoes, cleaning. A white fabric sofa near a dusty road will not stay white.

blocks.title: Worked example: a room assessment in 10 minutes
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi is asked by her neighbour to 'make the parlour nicer'. The parlour is about 4.5 m by 3.6 m, in a flat in Enugu, used for receiving visitors and for the family to watch TV in the evening.
steps: Function: visitors in the day, family TV in the evening, children sometimes do homework there.
Users: 2 adults, 3 children, frequent visitors from church.
Light: one window facing the road; one ceiling bulb with a cool white light. Dark corners after 6 pm.
Flow: a large centre table blocks the route from the door to the dining area; people walk sideways past it.
Clutter: school bags and shoes pile up by the door because there is nowhere to put them.
Colour: cream walls with marks at hand height; heavy brown curtains that are faded on the road side.
blocks.result: Ngozi's notes show the real problems are flow, storage, light and tired curtains. Her plan will start there, not with buying new decorations.

blocks.text: What clients usually pay a decorator for

Many first clients are friends, family, small shops, salons, offices and short-let apartment owners who want a space to look finished and welcoming without a large budget. What they value is your **eye** (knowing what to change), your **planning** (measuring correctly so things fit), your **sourcing** (knowing where to buy and what a fair price is) and your **reliability** (finishing on time and within budget). You do not need expensive software to start. A tape measure, a phone camera, a notebook and the skills in this course are enough.

blocks.title: Know your limits
blocks.text: Do not promise work that needs a licensed trade. Moving sockets, adding ceiling lights, removing walls or changing plumbing must be done by qualified people. You can coordinate them, but say clearly in writing that their work is their responsibility.

takeaways: Decoration works with the existing room; structural, electrical and plumbing work belongs to qualified trades
Always start with the room's function, its users and its current problems
Every job follows seven stages from brief to handover
Before photos from every corner protect you and build your portfolio

activity.title: Assess one real room
steps: Choose one room in your home or a friend's home.
Take before photos from each corner and from the doorway.
Write down the room's function, its users and when they use it.
Complete the five-point check: light, flow, clutter and storage, colour and condition, climate needs.
List the three biggest problems in order of importance.
activity.evidence: Your before photos and a one-page room assessment note

lessons.title: Design principles: balance, scale, proportion and focal point
objectives: Recognise symmetrical, asymmetrical and radial balance in a room
Choose furniture and decor of the right scale for a room and for each other
Create one clear focal point and arrange seating around it
Use rhythm and contrast to tie a room together

blocks.text: Design principles are the reasons a room feels calm or chaotic, cosy or cramped. Once you know them, you can explain to a client **why** a change works, which builds trust. This lesson covers the four you will use every day: balance, scale and proportion, focal point, and rhythm with contrast.

blocks.name: couch-and-lamp
blocks.alt: A sofa with a floor lamp beside it
blocks.caption: Even a sofa and one lamp can be arranged to feel balanced or lopsided.

blocks.text: Balance: spreading visual weight

Every object has **visual weight**. Large, dark, bright or heavily patterned things look heavier than small, light, plain ones. A room feels balanced when the visual weight is spread so that no side seems to tip over.

blocks.title: Two main ways to balance a room
items: Symmetrical balance
Asymmetrical balance
right: One sofa balanced by two chairs
blocks.caption: Both work; choose by the mood the client wants and the furniture they already own.

blocks.text: There is also **radial balance**, where items circle a centre, such as chairs around a round dining table or cushions around a pouffe. It is useful in small square rooms.
Scale and proportion: right size for the room

**Scale** is how big an object is compared with the room and with people. **Proportion** is how objects relate to each other. A huge three-seater and two armchairs will swallow a small parlour. A tiny picture on a wide wall looks lost. Practical guides decorators often use:

items: A coffee or centre table is often about two-thirds the length of the sofa, so people can reach it from each seat.
Art above a sofa is commonly about two-thirds to three-quarters of the sofa's width, hung with a gap of roughly 15 to 25 cm above the backrest.
Hang curtain rods higher and wider than the window frame to make windows and ceilings look bigger.
In a small room, choose furniture with visible legs and lighter colours; it lets the floor show and feels less heavy.
Mix sizes: a room with only small items looks fussy, and a room with only big items looks crowded.

blocks.text: Focal point: where the eye goes first

A focal point is the first thing you notice when you enter. Without one, the eye wanders and the room feels unfinished. With too many, the room feels noisy. Good focal points include a large window with a view, a feature wall painted in a deeper colour, a striking piece of art or fabric such as a framed adire or aso-oke panel, a TV wall that is styled neatly, or a bed with a strong headboard. Arrange the main seating to face or frame the focal point, and keep other walls quieter.
Rhythm and contrast

**Rhythm** means repeating a colour, shape or material so the eye moves around the room: the same green in the cushions, a plant and a picture frame. **Contrast** gives life: a smooth wall beside a woven raffia basket, a dark wood table on a light rug. A useful habit is to repeat each accent colour at least three times in a room.

blocks.title: Worked example: fixing a lopsided parlour
blocks.context: For example, Halima's client in Kano has a parlour about 4.8 m by 3.9 m. All the heavy furniture (a large sofa, a tall dark cabinet and the TV) sits on one long wall. The opposite wall is bare.
steps: Identify the problem: all the visual weight is on one side, and there is no clear focal point.
Choose the TV wall as the focal point, because the family watches TV every evening.
Move the tall cabinet to the opposite wall to balance the TV wall.
Place the sofa facing the TV, about 2.5 to 3 m from the screen, with two armchairs at the sides (asymmetrical balance).
Check scale: the old centre table was 1.4 m long against a 2.1 m sofa; swap it for the family's smaller 1.2 m table from the dining area, closer to two-thirds of the sofa length.
Repeat the client's favourite teal in three places: two cushions, a vase and a framed print.
blocks.result: The room now has one focal point, the weight is spread across both long walls, and nothing new was bought except one framed print.

blocks.text: Common mistakes to avoid

items: Pushing every piece of furniture against the walls, leaving an empty middle that feels like a waiting room. Pull seats in to form a conversation group.
Two competing focal points, such as a loud patterned wall opposite a large TV. Choose one and quieten the other.
Rugs that are too small, floating in the middle of the floor. Ideally at least the front legs of the sofa and chairs rest on the rug.
Hanging pictures too high. Many decorators aim for the centre of a picture at roughly eye level, about 1.5 m from the floor.

blocks.title: The squint test
blocks.text: Stand in the doorway and half close your eyes. Dark and heavy shapes stand out. If they all cluster on one side, the room is unbalanced. Take a photo and look at it in black and white on your phone for the same effect.

takeaways: Balance spreads visual weight; it can be symmetrical, asymmetrical or radial
Scale and proportion keep furniture right for the room and for each other
Give every room one clear focal point and arrange seating around it
Repeat accent colours about three times to create rhythm

activity.title: Rebalance one room on paper
steps: Photograph a room from the doorway and convert the photo to black and white.
Circle the heaviest items and decide whether the room is balanced.
Name the current focal point, or write 'none'.
Suggest two moves that improve balance or focal point without buying anything.
If possible, make one move and photograph the result from the same spot.
activity.evidence: Before and after photos with a short note of your two suggested moves

lessons.title: Colour: the colour wheel, schemes and the 60-30-10 rule
objectives: Name primary, secondary and tertiary colours on the colour wheel
Build monochromatic, analogous, complementary and triadic schemes
Apply the 60-30-10 proportion to walls, furniture and accents
Test paint colours properly before a client commits

blocks.text: Colour is the cheapest way to change a room and the easiest way to get it wrong. The colour wheel gives you a reliable method, so you are not just guessing or copying.

blocks.name: color-palette
blocks.alt: A person choosing colours from a palette
blocks.caption: A scheme chosen from the colour wheel looks planned, not accidental.

blocks.text: The colour wheel in two minutes

items: **Primary colours:** red, yellow and blue.
**Secondary colours:** made by mixing two primaries: orange (red + yellow), green (yellow + blue), purple (blue + red).
**Tertiary colours:** a primary mixed with a neighbouring secondary, such as yellow-green or red-orange. That makes 12 colours on the wheel.
**Warm colours** (reds, oranges, yellows) feel energetic and seem to come closer. **Cool colours** (blues, greens, purples) feel calm and seem to move away.
**Tint** = colour plus white (lighter). **Shade** = colour plus black (darker). **Tone** = colour plus grey (softer). Most wall paints are tints or tones, not pure colours.

blocks.text: Four schemes you can use

blocks.title: Choosing a colour scheme
items: Monochromatic: calm, simple
Analogous: harmonious, warm or cool
Complementary: lively, high contrast
Triadic: playful, needs care
axes: Number of colours: few to many
blocks.caption: Low-contrast schemes suit bedrooms; higher contrast suits shops, salons and children's rooms.

head: Scheme
How to build it
Example
rows: One colour in different tints, tones and shades
Pale sage walls, deeper green curtains, dark green cushions
Yellow, yellow-orange and orange in a warm dining room
Soft blue walls with burnt orange cushions
One colour plus the two neighbours of its opposite
Blue with yellow-orange and red-orange accents
Three colours evenly spaced on the wheel
Muted red, yellow and blue in a children's play corner

blocks.text: The 60-30-10 rule

A widely used guide is to divide a room's colour roughly into **60% dominant colour** (usually walls and large surfaces), **30% secondary colour** (sofa, curtains, a rug) and **10% accent colour** (cushions, vases, art, a throw). It is a guide, not a law, but it stops a room looking flat or chaotic. Neutrals such as white, cream, grey, beige and brown can fill the 60% so that the client's favourite bold colour can shine as the 10%.

blocks.title: Worked example: a scheme from a client's favourite fabric
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Abeokuta has a client who loves an adire fabric in indigo blue with small rust-orange details. The bedroom is about 3.6 m by 3.3 m and gets afternoon sun.
steps: Find the fabric colours on the wheel: indigo (blue) and rust (red-orange), almost opposites, so this is a complementary scheme.
60%: walls in a soft, warm off-white, so the afternoon sun does not make the room feel hotter, and the fabric stands out.
30%: indigo adire curtains and a plain mid-blue bedspread.
10%: rust-orange cushions, a clay pot and a picture frame, repeating the accent three times.
Check: low-contrast walls keep the bedroom calm; the complementary accents give life.
blocks.result: The scheme is planned around a fabric the client already loves, follows 60-30-10, and every colour choice has a reason she can explain.

blocks.text: Light changes colour

The same paint looks different in a room with strong afternoon sun, under a cool white bulb at night and under a warm white bulb. Dark colours make small rooms feel smaller unless the room has good light. Very bright colours on every wall can feel tiring. In hot, sunny rooms many people prefer cooler or lighter walls; in rooms used mostly at night, warmer tones often feel more welcoming.

items: Narrow the choice to two or three paint colours from the paint shop's colour card.
Buy small sample tins or ask the shop to mix a small quantity where possible.
Paint a patch about the size of an A3 sheet on two different walls, or on white card you can move around.
Look at it in the morning, afternoon and at night with the room's normal bulbs on.
Choose with the client only after seeing the patches in all three conditions, and write down the paint brand, colour name and code.

blocks.text: Working with colours the client already owns

Most clients will not replace everything. Start your scheme from what must stay: a brown leather sofa, a red rug from a relative, cream floor tiles. Brown, cream and tile colours usually act as neutrals. Find the strongest fixed colour on the wheel and build around it. If a client owns many unrelated colours, choose one to lead, repeat it, and let the others recede by moving some items to other rooms or covering them with plain throws and cushion covers.

blocks.title: Never choose from a phone screen alone
blocks.text: Phone and computer screens show colours differently from real paint and fabric. Use online palettes for ideas, then confirm with real samples in the real room.

blocks.title: Paint safely
blocks.text: Keep windows and doors open while painting and until the smell fades, take breaks in fresh air, and keep paint and thinners away from children and from flames. Read the safety instructions on the tin and choose low-odour, water-based paint for bedrooms where possible.

takeaways: The colour wheel has 3 primary, 3 secondary and 6 tertiary colours
Monochromatic and analogous schemes feel calm; complementary and triadic feel lively
Use roughly 60% dominant, 30% secondary and 10% accent colour
Test real paint patches in morning, afternoon and night light before choosing

activity.title: Build a colour scheme
steps: Pick one fabric, picture or object the room's owner loves.
Identify its two or three main colours and find them on a colour wheel.
Name the scheme (monochromatic, analogous, complementary, split complementary or triadic).
Assign colours to the 60%, 30% and 10% parts of the room.
Collect real samples (paint card chips, fabric offcuts) and photograph them together in the room.
activity.evidence: A photo of your physical sample board with the 60-30-10 plan written beside it

quiz.q: A client asks you to move a ceiling light point to the centre of the room. What should you do?
options: Bring in a qualified electrician and coordinate the work
Do the wiring yourself to save the client money
Tell the client it is impossible
Hide the old light with a curtain
quiz.explain: Electrical changes are structural work for a qualified electrician. A decorator coordinates, but does not do licensed trade work.

quiz.q: What should a decorator do first on a new job?
options: Find out the room's function, users and problems, and take before photos
quiz.explain: Function, users and problems guide every later choice, and before photos are needed for planning and the portfolio.

quiz.q: A parlour has a large sofa, dark cabinet and TV all on one wall and a bare opposite wall. Which principle is broken?
quiz.explain: All the visual weight sits on one side, so the room is unbalanced. Moving a heavy item to the opposite wall helps.

quiz.q: Using the common guide, about how long should a centre table be for a 2.1 m sofa?
quiz.explain: Two-thirds of 2.1 m is 1.4 m, so a table of roughly 1.2 to 1.4 m suits the sofa.

quiz.q: Soft blue walls with burnt orange cushions is an example of which scheme?
quiz.explain: Blue and orange sit opposite each other on the colour wheel, which makes a complementary scheme.

quiz.q: In the 60-30-10 rule, what usually takes the 10%?
options: Accents such as cushions, vases and art
quiz.explain: The 10% is the accent colour, carried by small items repeated around the room.

quiz.q: Why should a client see paint patches at night as well as in daylight?
options: Bulbs change how colours look, and the room may be used mostly at night
It makes the paint last longer
quiz.explain: Colour depends on light. A colour that looks right in afternoon sun may look different under the room's bulbs.

modules.title: Guided practice: measure, plan, light and dress the room
modules.overview: This module turns ideas into numbers. You will measure a room and draw it to scale, plan layered lighting that still works during power cuts, and calculate exactly how much fabric curtains and soft furnishings need.

lessons.title: Measuring a room and drawing a simple floor plan to scale
objectives: Measure walls, windows, doors, sockets and ceiling height accurately
Draw a floor plan at a scale of 1:50 on graph paper
Test furniture layouts with paper cut-outs before moving anything
Check walkway clearances using common spacing guides

blocks.text: Most expensive decorating mistakes are measuring mistakes: a sofa that will not pass through the door, curtains 20 cm too short, a rug that covers a floor socket. A simple floor plan prevents them. You need a **5 m or 8 m steel tape measure**, a pencil, a notebook, graph paper with 1 cm squares, a ruler and your phone camera. A helper makes it faster.

blocks.name: triangular-ruler
blocks.caption: A ruler, graph paper and a tape measure are all you need to draw an accurate plan.

blocks.text: Step 1: Sketch, then measure

items: Stand in the doorway and draw a rough outline of the room in your notebook. It does not need to be neat. Mark the door, windows, sockets, switches, AC units, pillars and anything fixed.
Start at one corner and work clockwise. Measure each wall along the floor from corner to corner and write the number on that wall in your sketch, in centimetres.
For each window, measure its width, its height, the distance from the nearest corner, and the height of the sill from the floor.
For each door, measure the width and the distance from the corner, and draw the curve of the door swing. Furniture cannot sit inside that curve.
Measure the ceiling height in at least one place, and note sockets and switches with their distance from a corner.
Photograph each wall so you can check details later.

blocks.title: Check your numbers
blocks.text: Opposite walls in a rectangular room should be nearly the same length. If one wall is 360 cm and the opposite is 342 cm, measure both again. Also add up the pieces of each wall (corner to window, window width, window to corner) and check the total equals the full wall length.

blocks.title: Ladders and high measuring
blocks.text: Use a stable step ladder on a flat floor, never a plastic chair or a stool on a table. Have someone hold the ladder, keep three points of contact, and do not lean far to the side. Keep the tape away from ceiling fans and switch them off.
Step 2: Draw to scale

A scale drawing shrinks every measurement by the same amount. The most practical scale for rooms is **1:50**: 1 cm on paper stands for 50 cm in the room, so **2 cm on paper = 1 m** in real life. On 1 cm graph paper, each square is 50 cm. To convert, divide the real measurement in centimetres by 50.

blocks.title: Worked example: a bedroom at 1:50
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka measures a bedroom in Port Harcourt: 420 cm by 360 cm, ceiling 270 cm. The door is 90 cm wide, 20 cm from the left corner of the 360 cm wall. The window is 150 cm wide, centred on the opposite 360 cm wall, sill 90 cm from the floor.
steps: Long walls: 420 ÷ 50 = 8.4 cm on paper. Short walls: 360 ÷ 50 = 7.2 cm.
Door: 90 ÷ 50 = 1.8 cm wide, placed 20 ÷ 50 = 0.4 cm from the corner, with a quarter circle of radius 1.8 cm for the swing.
Window: 150 ÷ 50 = 3 cm wide. The wall is 7.2 cm, so it starts (7.2 − 3) ÷ 2 = 2.1 cm from each corner.
Floor area for later costing: 4.2 m × 3.6 m = 15.12 square metres (m²).
Write the scale (1:50), the room name and the date in the corner of the drawing.
blocks.result: An 8.4 cm by 7.2 cm drawing that fits on one page and shows every opening accurately, ready for furniture cut-outs.

blocks.text: Step 3: Plan furniture with cut-outs

Measure each piece of furniture (width and depth), draw it at the same 1:50 scale on card, cut it out and label it. A 200 cm by 90 cm sofa becomes a 4 cm by 1.8 cm rectangle. A double bed of about 137 cm by 190 cm becomes about 2.7 cm by 3.8 cm. Slide the pieces around the plan until the layout works, then photograph the best two options to show the client. Free floor plan apps can do the same on a phone, but paper is quick and needs no data.

blocks.title: Layout checks before you move furniture
items: Doors open fully
Main walkway about 90 cm
Sockets reachable, not blocked
Windows can open
Seats face the focal point
blocks.caption: Run every layout through these checks on paper first.

blocks.text: Spacing guides decorators commonly use

head: Space
Common guide (approximate)
rows: About 90 cm; at least about 60 cm for a minor route
About 40 to 45 cm, close enough to reach a cup
Beside and at the foot of a bed
About 60 cm or more to walk and make the bed
In front of a wardrobe or drawers
Enough to open doors fully and stand, often 75 cm or more
About 75 to 90 cm from table edge to the wall

blocks.text: These are guides, not rules. In a small Nigerian flat you may have to accept less in one place to gain storage elsewhere. Always check that the client's actual furniture fits through the door, along the corridor and up the stairs: measure the narrowest point of the route, and compare it with the furniture's depth and height, not only its width.

takeaways: Sketch first, then measure clockwise and record everything in centimetres
At 1:50, 2 cm on paper equals 1 m in the room; divide centimetres by 50
Test layouts with scale cut-outs before moving heavy furniture
Keep main walkways around 90 cm and never block doors, sockets or windows

activity.title: Draw one room to scale
steps: Sketch a room and mark doors, windows, sockets and fixed items.
Measure every wall, opening and the ceiling height and record them on the sketch.
Draw the room at 1:50 on graph paper with the door swing shown.
Make scale cut-outs of the main furniture and try two layouts.
Check each layout against the five layout checks and photograph the better one.
activity.evidence: Your measured sketch, the 1:50 floor plan and a photo of your preferred layout

lessons.title: Lighting layers: ambient, task and accent light
objectives: Explain the three layers of lighting and what each is for
Choose bulbs by lumens and colour temperature instead of watts
Plan lighting that still works during power cuts
Follow basic electrical safety and know when to call an electrician

blocks.text: One bright bulb in the centre of the ceiling is the most common lighting in homes, and it is why many rooms feel flat at night. Professionals plan light in **layers**, so the room works for every activity and has depth and warmth.

blocks.name: electric-light-bulb
blocks.caption: Choosing the right bulb, by lumens and colour temperature, changes a room more than many decorations.

blocks.text: The three layers

blocks.title: Layers of light in a room
items: Accent: highlights and mood
Task: light for activities
Ambient: general light
blocks.caption: Start with ambient light at the base, add task light where people work, then accent light for atmosphere.

items: **Ambient (general) light** fills the room so people can move safely: ceiling lights, daylight from windows, wall lights that bounce light upward.
**Task light** is brighter, focused light for a job: a reading lamp beside a chair, a desk lamp for homework, under-cabinet light over a kitchen counter, a light either side of a mirror for make-up.
**Accent light** creates mood and draws attention: a small lamp on a side table, a strip light behind a TV, a spotlight on art or a plant.

blocks.text: Read the bulb box: lumens and kelvin

**Lumens (lm)** measure how much light a bulb gives. Watts measure how much power it uses. With LED bulbs, compare lumens, not watts. As a common reference, an LED of about 800 lumens gives roughly the same light as an old 60 W filament bulb while using far less power, which matters when you run on an inverter, solar system or generator.

head: Colour temperature
Looks like
Good for
rows: Detailed work, workshops; can feel harsh in a bedroom

blocks.text: Kelvin (K) is printed on the box. Mixing very different colour temperatures in one room can look patchy, so try to keep them similar within a space. Many homes use cool daylight bulbs everywhere because they look bright; switching living and bedroom lamps to warm white is one of the cheapest changes you can suggest.
Natural light and power cuts

Use daylight first. Keep windows clear of heavy furniture, use lighter curtains or sheers by day, and place mirrors where they reflect a window. For evenings with unstable power, plan at least one light in each layer that runs on the inverter or solar circuit, or use rechargeable LED lamps for task and accent light. Rechargeable lamps and battery string lights also avoid long extension cables across the floor.

blocks.title: Worked example: a lighting plan for a small parlour
blocks.context: For example, Funke's client in Ibadan has a parlour of about 4 m by 3.5 m lit only by one cool daylight ceiling bulb. The family reads, watches TV and receives guests there in the evening.
steps: Ambient: replace the ceiling bulb with a warm white LED of about 1000 to 1500 lumens, or two smaller fittings if the electrician can add a point.
Task: one reading floor lamp beside the armchair with a warm white bulb of about 800 lumens, plugged into an existing socket.
Accent: a small rechargeable table lamp on the side cabinet and a warm LED strip behind the TV to reduce glare.
Power cuts: the ceiling light and TV strip are on the inverter circuit; the table lamp is rechargeable.
Safety: no new extension cables across walkways; the electrician checks the socket load.
blocks.result: Three layers of light, a warmer evening feel, and the room still works when public power goes off.

blocks.title: Electrical safety
blocks.text: Never do wiring yourself or let an unqualified person do it. Use a qualified electrician for new points, ceiling fittings and inverter connections. Do not overload sockets or extension boxes, do not run cables under rugs where they can overheat or be damaged, keep lamps and bulbs away from curtains and fabrics, and buy fittings and cables from reputable sellers rather than the cheapest unbranded ones.
Lighting by room

head: Room
Ambient
Task
Accent
rows: Table lamp, TV backlight, light on art
Bedside lamps on both sides; mirror light
Light over the counter and cooker
Bright light at the work chair or counter
Spotlight on displays and the sign

blocks.text: Fit lampshades that suit the job: an opaque shade pushes light down for reading, a fabric or paper shade spreads a soft glow. Dimmable bulbs only work with a compatible dimmer switch, so check the box and ask the electrician before promising a dimming effect.

blocks.title: Light the corners
blocks.text: A room feels bigger and more welcoming when its corners are lit. One lamp in a dark corner often does more than a brighter ceiling bulb.

takeaways: Plan ambient, task and accent light for every room
Compare LED bulbs by lumens; about 800 lumens is roughly an old 60 W bulb
Warm white (about 2700 to 3000 K) suits living rooms and bedrooms
Plan for power cuts and leave all wiring to a qualified electrician

activity.title: Map the light in one room
steps: List every light source in a room, including windows, and label each as ambient, task or accent.
Read the box or bulb for lumens and kelvin, where available.
Note which lights work during a power cut.
Mark on your floor plan where one task light and one accent light should go.
Photograph the room at night before and, if possible, after one change.
activity.evidence: Your labelled light list and a floor plan marked with proposed lights

lessons.title: Curtains and soft furnishings: measuring and fabric calculations
objectives: Measure a window for curtains correctly from the track or rod
Calculate the number of fabric widths and total metres needed
Adjust a calculation for pattern repeat
Estimate fabric for cushion covers and choose the right rug size

blocks.text: Curtains, cushions, throws and rugs are called **soft furnishings**. They add colour, texture, privacy and sound absorption, and they are often the biggest single cost in a budget makeover. Calculating fabric correctly saves the client money and saves you embarrassment at the tailor's.

blocks.name: window
blocks.caption: Curtain fabric is calculated from the track width and the drop, not from the window frame alone.

blocks.text: Key words

items: **Track or rod width:** the length of the curtain track or pole. It usually extends beyond the window frame, often about 15 to 20 cm each side, so open curtains do not block light.
**Finished drop:** how long the finished curtain hangs, from the track or rod to where it ends (floor, sill or below the sill).
**Cut drop:** finished drop plus extra for the heading at the top and the hem at the bottom. Allow about 25 to 30 cm in total unless your tailor says otherwise.

**Fullness:** how much wider the fabric is than the track, so the curtain falls in folds. Gathered and pencil pleat curtains are commonly about 2 to 2.5 times the track; eyelet curtains about 1.5 to 2 times.
**Fabric width:** the width of the fabric roll, printed on the bolt or tag. Curtain fabrics are often around 140 cm wide, but some are much wider, so always check.
**Pattern repeat:** the distance before a printed pattern repeats down the fabric.

blocks.text: The formula

blocks.title: Curtain fabric in four steps
items: Track width × fullness
÷ fabric width, round up
× cut drop
= total metres
blocks.caption: Always round the number of widths up to a whole number, because fabric is cut in full widths.

blocks.title: Worked example: living room curtains
blocks.context: For example, Aisha's client in Abuja has a window 1.5 m wide. The track will be 1.8 m (15 cm past the frame each side). Floor-length pencil pleat curtains, with the track 2.4 m above the floor. Plain fabric, 1.4 m wide.
steps: Finished drop: 2.4 m, minus about 1 cm so the curtain just clears the floor, so about 2.39 m. Use 2.4 m for simple calculation.
Cut drop: 2.4 m + 0.3 m allowance = 2.7 m.
Fabric needed across: 1.8 m × fullness 2 = 3.6 m.
Number of widths: 3.6 ÷ 1.4 = 2.57, rounded up to 3 widths (split between a pair of curtains, one and a half widths each).
Total fabric: 3 widths × 2.7 m = 8.1 m.

Costing (approximate, for illustration only): if the fabric sells for about ₦4,000 per metre at the market, 8.1 m is about ₦32,400 before lining, tape and tailoring. Check current prices at your market.
blocks.result: Buy about 8.1 m, or round to 8.5 m to allow for any shrinkage or a cutting mistake if the seller cuts by the half metre.

blocks.text: Patterned fabric

With a pattern, each width must start at the same point of the pattern so the design lines up across the curtains. Round the cut drop up to a whole number of repeats. In the example above, if the pattern repeat is 64 cm, the cut drop of 270 cm becomes 5 repeats (5 × 64 = 320 cm), because 4 repeats (256 cm) is too short. The total becomes 3 × 3.2 m = 9.6 m. Patterned fabric always needs more metres, so tell the client before they choose.

blocks.title: Shrinkage and lining
blocks.text: Some cotton fabrics shrink when washed. Ask the seller, or wash a small piece first. Lining protects curtains from strong sun fading and improves privacy; it is calculated the same way, usually without pattern repeat.
Cushions and rugs

items: **Cushion cover (envelope style) for a 45 cm cushion:** cut one piece about 47 cm by about 115 cm (front plus two overlapping back flaps plus seams). From fabric 140 cm wide, about 0.5 m is enough for one cover, with the 115 cm length laid across the fabric width. For four covers, buy about 2 m and confirm the layout with your tailor.
**Cushion sizes:** 40 cm, 45 cm and 50 cm squares are common; make covers to fit the inner cushion snugly so it looks full.
**Rugs in a living room:** choose a size where at least the front legs of the sofa and chairs sit on the rug. A rug that floats in the middle makes the room look smaller.
**Rugs under a bed:** the rug should extend beyond the sides of the bed, often about 45 to 60 cm, so feet land on it in the morning.

blocks.title: Measure the actual track, not the window
blocks.text: If the track is not yet installed, agree its exact length and height with the client and the fitter first, then calculate. A track raised by 20 cm changes the drop and the metres for every curtain.

blocks.title: Fabric and fire
blocks.text: Keep curtains and throws well away from cookers, candles, mosquito coils, lanterns and hot bulbs. Tie back long curtains near kitchen windows, and keep cords of blinds out of children's reach.

takeaways: Widths = track width × fullness ÷ fabric width, always rounded up
Cut drop = finished drop + about 25 to 30 cm for heading and hem
Total fabric = widths × cut drop; patterned fabric needs drops rounded to whole repeats
Rugs should be big enough for front furniture legs to sit on them

activity.title: Calculate curtains for a real window
steps: Measure the track or agree its width and height for one window.
Decide floor, sill or below-sill length and record the finished drop.
Check the fabric width at a shop or market and choose a fullness.
Calculate widths, cut drop and total metres, and repeat for a patterned option.
Ask for the price per metre and write an approximate fabric cost.
activity.evidence: A calculation sheet showing both plain and patterned fabric totals with the shop's price per metre

quiz.q: At a scale of 1:50, how long should a 420 cm wall be on paper?
quiz.explain: Divide centimetres by 50: 420 ÷ 50 = 8.4 cm.

quiz.q: Opposite walls of a rectangular room measure 360 cm and 342 cm. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, it does not matter
quiz.explain: Opposite walls should be nearly equal. A big difference usually means a measuring mistake, so re-measure.

quiz.q: A client's parlour feels flat at night with one ceiling bulb. Which addition gives task light?
options: A warm LED strip behind the TV
A reading lamp beside the armchair
quiz.explain: Task light is focused light for an activity, such as reading. The TV strip is accent light and the ceiling bulb is ambient.

quiz.q: Which bulb suits a bedroom best for a cosy feel?
options: The bulb with the highest watts
quiz.explain: Warm white at about 2700 to 3000 K gives a soft, cosy light suited to bedrooms and living rooms.

quiz.q: Track 2 m, fullness 2, fabric 1.4 m wide, cut drop 2.6 m. How much plain fabric is needed?
Cut drop is 270 cm and the pattern repeat is 64 cm. What cut drop should you use?
quiz.explain: Round up to whole repeats: 4 repeats is 256 cm (too short), so use 5 repeats, 320 cm.

quiz.q: Why should you not run extension cables under a rug?
options: It is illegal to own extension cables
They can overheat or be damaged unseen, which is a fire risk
quiz.explain: Covered cables can overheat and damage cannot be seen, creating a fire and shock risk.

modules.title: Quality and evidence: budgets, finishing and proof of results
modules.overview: Most clients have modest budgets. This module shows how to get the biggest change for the least money using paint, rearranging and local materials, how to finish work to a professional and safe standard, and how to record results so you can prove what you achieved.

lessons.title: Budget makeovers with paint, rearranging and local materials
objectives: Rank makeover changes by impact and cost
Calculate how much paint a room needs
Build a makeover budget with a contingency
Use local materials such as adire, ankara, raffia, cane and clay creatively

blocks.text: A budget makeover is not a cheap-looking room. It is a room where every naira went to the change that made the biggest difference. Your job is to spend in the right order.

blocks.name: painting-the-room
blocks.alt: A person painting a wall with a roller
blocks.caption: Paint is usually the change with the biggest impact for the lowest cost.

blocks.text: Spend in this order

blocks.title: Impact versus cost
items: Do first: declutter, rearrange, paint
Plan for: curtains, lighting, rug
Quick wins: cushions, plants, art
Avoid on a tight budget: new big furniture
blocks.caption: Top-left is free or cheap and changes the most; bottom-right costs the most for the least change.

items: **Declutter and clean:** remove what is broken, unused or belongs in another room. This is free and often the biggest change.
**Rearrange:** use your floor plan to create a better layout and focal point with existing furniture.
**Paint:** fresh walls, or one feature wall, transform a room for a modest cost.
**Light:** warm bulbs and one or two lamps (Module 2).
**Soft furnishings:** new curtains, cushion covers and a throw in the planned colour scheme.
**Accessories:** plants, framed prints, baskets and mirrors to finish.
**Replace furniture** only if a piece is broken, unsafe or completely the wrong size.

blocks.text: How much paint?

Wall area = perimeter of the room × wall height, minus doors and windows. Then multiply by the number of coats (usually two) and divide by the **coverage** printed on the tin, in square metres per litre. Coverage varies by brand, product and wall surface, so always read the tin; new or porous plaster usually needs more paint or a primer coat.

blocks.title: Worked example: painting a bedroom
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma is painting the 4.2 m by 3.6 m bedroom from Module 2, ceiling 2.7 m, with one door (0.9 m by 2.1 m) and one window (1.5 m by 1.2 m). The tin she chooses says coverage is about 10 m² per litre per coat.
steps: Gross wall area: 15.6 × 2.7 = 42.1 m².
Openings: door 0.9 × 2.1 = 1.9 m²; window 1.5 × 1.2 = 1.8 m²; total 3.7 m².
Net area: 42.1 − 3.7 = 38.4 m². Two coats: 76.8 m².
Litres: 76.8 ÷ 10 = 7.7 litres, so she buys enough for about 8 litres, plus a little for touch-ups.
Feature wall option: paint only the 3.6 m bed wall in a deeper colour: 3.6 × 2.7 = 9.7 m², two coats = 19.4 m², about 2 litres.
blocks.result: About 8 litres for the whole room, or about 2 litres if the client chooses a single feature wall, which costs far less and still changes the room.

blocks.text: Local materials that look good and cost less

items: **Adire, ankara and aso-oke:** cushion covers, a table runner, a framed fabric panel as wall art, or a headboard covered in fabric. Offcuts from tailors can be enough for cushions.
**Raffia, cane and rattan:** baskets for storage (solving the clutter problem), lampshades, chairs and room dividers from local weavers.
**Clay pots, calabash and carved wood:** accent pieces and planters that repeat warm earth colours.
**Plants:** snake plant, pothos and other hardy plants add life; check they suit the light and are safe if there are small children or pets who might chew leaves.
**Upcycling:** sand and repaint an old side table or cabinet, change handles, or reupholster a chair seat with new foam and fabric.

blocks.text: Build the budget

head: Item
Quantity
Approx. unit cost (₦)
Approx. total (₦)
rows: Warm LED bulbs and one lamp

blocks.text: Prices change quickly and vary by city and market, so treat every figure in this course as an illustration. Get at least two prices for each major item, write the seller's name and date beside each price, and add a **contingency** of around 10% for price rises, transport and small surprises such as a missing curtain hook or an extra tin of paint.

blocks.title: Keep a sourcing list
blocks.text: Build your own list of fabric sellers, tailors, painters, weavers, carpenters and electricians, with phone numbers and the prices they quoted. Over time this list becomes one of the most valuable things you bring to a client.

blocks.title: Upcycling safely
blocks.text: Wear a dust mask and work outdoors or with windows open when sanding old furniture, because old paint may contain harmful substances. Keep thinners and spray paint away from flames and children, and let pieces dry fully before bringing them inside.

takeaways: Spend in order: declutter, rearrange, paint, light, soft furnishings, accessories, furniture
Paint litres = net wall area × coats ÷ coverage on the tin
Local fabrics, raffia, cane and clay give character at modest cost
Get two prices per major item and add about 10% contingency

activity.title: Plan a budget makeover
steps: Using your room assessment, list changes in the spend-in-this-order sequence.
Calculate paint for the full room and for a feature wall.
Collect at least two real prices for paint, fabric and one accessory, with seller and date.
Complete a budget table with a 10% contingency.
Choose which changes fit a budget the room owner gives you.
activity.evidence: A completed budget table with sources and dates for each price

lessons.title: Finishing to a professional, safe and honest standard
objectives: Inspect a finished room against a quality checklist
Apply safety precautions for children, older people, fire and heavy items
Handle client money, receipts and supplier commissions honestly
Respect client privacy in their home and in photos

blocks.text: Clients judge you by the details: a crooked curtain, a paint drip on the tiles, a wobbling shelf. They also judge you by honesty with their money. This lesson gives you a finishing standard and the safety and ethics habits that protect clients and your reputation.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.caption: Walk every room with a checklist before you call the client for handover.

blocks.text: The finishing checklist

blocks.title: Before you invite the client in
items: Paint edges clean, no drips
Curtains level, even folds
Art straight, at eye level
Cables hidden, sockets clear
Room cleaned, waste removed
blocks.caption: Check each item yourself; do not leave it for the client to find.

items: **Paint:** straight lines where wall meets ceiling and frames, no drips on floors or switches, even colour without patches. Remove masking tape before the paint is fully hard so the edge stays clean.
**Curtains:** track straight and secure, hems level and just clearing the floor, folds evenly spaced, curtains open and close smoothly.
**Furniture:** layout matches the agreed plan, doors and drawers open fully, nothing wobbles.
**Walls:** frames level (use a spirit level or a level app), hung at a consistent height, fixings suitable for the wall.
**Lighting:** every bulb works, colour temperatures match within the room, cables are tidy and not under rugs.
**Clean-up:** dust and paint spots removed, packaging and offcuts taken away, client's belongings put back.

blocks.text: Safety in the finished room

items: **Tall and heavy furniture:** wardrobes, bookcases and TV units can tip over onto children. Fix them to the wall with anti-tip straps or brackets, and secure TVs.
**Heavy mirrors and art:** use fixings rated for the weight and wall type (wall plugs and screws in block walls), not a single small nail.
**Fire:** keep fabrics away from cookers, candles and lamps; do not block exits or windows used for escape.
**Trips:** secure rug edges, avoid loose cables, keep walkways clear, especially for older people and anyone using a walking aid.
**Children:** blind and curtain cords out of reach; no small loose decorations they can swallow in a child's room.

blocks.title: Working at height and with tools
blocks.text: Use a stable ladder with a helper holding it, wear eye protection when drilling, check walls for hidden cables and pipes before drilling (they often run straight up or down from switches and sockets), and keep tools away from children during the work.
Honest practice with client money

Trust is your main asset. Agree in writing how you charge. If you buy materials for the client, keep every receipt and give copies. If a supplier offers you a commission or discount for bringing customers, tell the client and agree whether the saving goes to them or is part of your fee. Never quietly add a hidden mark-up to receipts. Return unused materials or money, or agree in writing what happens to leftovers.

blocks.title: Worked example: a transparent materials account
blocks.context: For example, Kemi receives ₦120,000 (illustrative figure) from a client in Lagos for materials. She buys curtain fabric, paint, bulbs and two baskets.
steps: She photographs each receipt immediately and saves it in a WhatsApp chat or folder for that client.
She records each purchase in a simple table: date, item, seller, amount.
Total spent is ₦108,500. Her fabric seller gave a ₦3,000 discount because Kemi is a regular customer; she shows it on the receipt as agreed.
She sends the client the table, receipt photos and the balance of ₦11,500, transferred back the same day or credited against her fee as agreed in writing.
blocks.result: The client can see every naira. Kemi's openness becomes the reason the client recommends her to two friends.

blocks.text: Privacy and respect

You are working inside someone's home. Ask permission before photographing any room, and agree in writing whether you may post photos publicly. Before posting, remove or blur family photos, documents, house numbers, children's faces and anything that shows the location or valuables. Never share a client's address or details of their home with other people. Store client data on your phone securely and delete what you no longer need.
The handover walk-through

items: Walk the client through the room in the same order as the brief, showing how each original problem was solved.
Show how to open and close curtains, operate new lamps and care for fabrics (washing instructions, keeping them out of strong sun).
Hand over receipts, leftover paint labelled with the colour name and code for touch-ups, and the final account.
Ask the client to point out anything they are not happy with, agree what you will fix and by when, and write it down.
Thank them and agree when you will send the feedback questions.

blocks.title: Payment scams
blocks.text: Confirm that transfers have arrived in your bank app before releasing work or materials, because fake credit alerts by SMS are a known scam. Pay suppliers you have not used before only after seeing the goods or confirming them through people you trust.

takeaways: Inspect paint, curtains, furniture, walls, lighting and clean-up before handover
Anchor tall furniture, use correct wall fixings and keep fabrics away from heat
Keep and share every receipt and disclose supplier discounts or commissions
Get written permission before photographing or posting a client's home

activity.title: Run a quality and safety audit
steps: Walk through a room you decorated or arranged, using the finishing checklist.
Note every item that does not meet the standard and fix what you can.
Check for tip-over, trip, fire and child safety risks and list solutions.
Draft a short written note to a client on how you charge and handle receipts.
Write a one-paragraph photo permission request.
activity.evidence: A completed checklist with fixes noted, plus your money and photo permission notes

lessons.title: Documenting results: photos, budget tracking and client feedback
objectives: Take before and after photos that show a fair comparison
Track budget against actual spending and calculate the variance
Collect useful client feedback with simple questions
Write a one-page project report

blocks.text: Evidence turns a nice room into proof of your skill. Good records help you price better next time, show future clients what you can do, and complete the capstone of this course.

blocks.name: photo-session
blocks.caption: Before and after photos from the same spot are the core of your evidence.

blocks.text: Before and after photos that tell the truth

items: Take before photos from fixed spots: each corner and the doorway. Note or mark where you stood.
Hold the phone at the same height each time, about chest height, and keep it level. Use the phone's grid lines to keep walls straight.
Shoot in daylight with curtains open and, if needed, room lights on. Take the after photos at a similar time of day.
Do not use beauty filters or heavy editing. You may straighten and crop, but colours must look like the real room.
Add a few close-ups after the work: curtain heading, cushion detail, styled shelf.

blocks.title: What to record and when
items: Before: photos and assessment
Planning: plan and budget
During: receipts and changes
After: photos and checklist
Two weeks later: feedback
blocks.caption: Record at each stage, not only at the end.

blocks.text: Budget versus actual

**Variance** is the difference between what you planned to spend and what you actually spent. Calculate it for each line and for the total. A positive variance (spent more than planned) needs an explanation; patterns over several jobs show where your estimates are weak.

blocks.title: Worked example: tracking a makeover budget
blocks.context: For example, Zainab's plan for a parlour makeover in Kaduna had a budget of ₦150,000 (illustrative figures).
steps: Fabric: planned ₦45,000, actual ₦48,600. Variance +₦3,600, because she needed patterned fabric with a repeat.
Paint: planned ₦30,000, actual ₦27,000. Variance −₦3,000.
Lighting: planned ₦25,000, actual ₦25,000. Variance ₦0.
Tailoring and labour: planned ₦35,000, actual ₦38,000. Variance +₦3,000 for an extra cushion order.
Contingency: ₦15,000 planned. The lines together cost ₦138,600 against ₦135,000 planned, so ₦3,600 of the contingency was used.
Total actual: ₦138,600 against the full ₦150,000 budget. Variance −₦11,400, or about 7.6% under budget (11,400 ÷ 150,000 × 100 = 7.6%).
blocks.result: Zainab finished under budget, and she learned to check pattern repeat before quoting fabric next time.

blocks.text: Simple measures of success

head: Measure
How to record it
rows: Total actual vs total budget, as a percentage
Planned finish date vs actual finish date
Tick each problem from the original assessment that is now fixed
Score out of 5 from the feedback questions
Number of new enquiries that came from this client

blocks.text: Collecting feedback
Ask for feedback about two weeks after handover, when the client has lived in the room. Send short questions by WhatsApp or a free online form, and make it easy to be honest.

items: On a scale of 1 to 5, how happy are you with the room?
Which change has made the biggest difference to how you use the room?
Is there anything that does not work well now?
Was the work finished on time and within the budget we agreed?
May I quote your words, with your first name only, in my portfolio?

blocks.title: Make feedback easy
blocks.text: Send the questions as one short message the client can answer by voice note if they prefer. Thank them whatever they say, and save the reply in the client's folder.

blocks.title: Welcome criticism
blocks.text: A comment such as 'the curtains block too much light in the morning' is useful. Thank the client, fix it if you reasonably can, and record what you will do differently next time.
Organising your records

Create one folder per client on your phone or in Google Drive, named with the client's first name, area and month, for example 'Tola Yaba Mar'. Inside, keep four sub-folders: Before, Plan, Receipts and After. Save the brief, floor plan, budget and feedback in the Plan folder. Back up the folder, because a lost phone should not mean lost evidence. Keep client folders private, and do not upload them to public places.
Learning from several jobs

After three or four projects, compare your records. Do you always underestimate tailoring? Do jobs always run a week late because fabric delivery is slow? Do clients rate lighting changes highly? These patterns tell you how to quote more accurately, which suppliers to change, and which services to promote. Add one line to each report called 'What I will do differently next time' and read these lines before you quote the next job.
The one-page project report

Put it together on one page or one Canva design: the client brief in two lines, the main problems, three before and after photo pairs, the colour scheme and why, budget versus actual, time taken, and the client's feedback. This becomes a portfolio page and your evidence for the capstone.

takeaways: Shoot before and after photos from the same spots, height and time of day, without filters
Variance = actual minus planned; explain every overspend
Measure success by budget, time, problems solved, satisfaction and referrals
Ask for feedback about two weeks after handover

activity.title: Document one project
steps: Choose a room you have improved, even a small change.
Take after photos from the same spots as your before photos.
Fill in a budget versus actual table and calculate the total variance.
Send the five feedback questions to the room owner.
Make a one-page report with photos, numbers and feedback.
activity.evidence: Your one-page project report with before and after pairs

quiz.q: A client has ₦40,000 (illustrative) and a cluttered, dark parlour with old cream walls. What should come first?
options: Declutter and rearrange, then paint or warm bulbs
quiz.explain: Free and low-cost changes with high impact come first; new big furniture is the least efficient use of a small budget.

quiz.q: Net wall area is 38.4 m², two coats, and the tin covers 10 m² per litre. How much paint is needed?
Why add about 10% contingency to a makeover budget?
options: To cover price rises, transport and small surprises
To pay for the client's furniture
quiz.explain: Prices and small needs change during a job; a contingency stops the project stalling.

quiz.q: A fabric seller gives you a discount for bringing a client. What is the honest approach?
options: Keep it and show the full price on the receipt
Ask the seller for a fake receipt
Tell the client and handle it as you agreed
quiz.explain: Disclosing discounts and commissions and agreeing how they are handled keeps trust.

quiz.q: Which is the most important safety step for a tall bookcase in a family home?
options: Fix it to the wall with an anti-tip strap or bracket
Put heavy items on the top shelf
quiz.explain: Tall furniture can tip onto children; anchoring it to the wall prevents this.

quiz.q: Planned budget ₦150,000, actual spend ₦142,200. What is the result?
Which makes after photos a fair comparison?
options: Same spots, same height and similar time of day as the before photos
A beauty filter to brighten the room
Photos taken at night with flash
quiz.explain: Matching position, height and light makes the comparison honest and convincing.

modules.title: Portfolio and impact: client brief, quotation and your decorating business
modules.overview: This module prepares you to work with paying clients. You will run a proper client brief and site visit, write a clear itemised quotation with payment terms, and present your work in a portfolio that wins the next job.

lessons.title: The client brief and site visit
objectives: Run a structured client brief using a standard question list
Capture budget, timeline, must-keep items and style preferences in writing
Turn a brief into a simple mood board and concept
Confirm the brief with the client before quoting

blocks.text: The **client brief** is the agreed description of what the client wants, why, for how much and by when. A weak brief causes most disputes: 'I said modern, not this.' A strong brief makes every later decision easier, and it is the document you go back to when a client changes their mind.

blocks.name: meeting
blocks.alt: Two people in a meeting discussing plans
blocks.caption: A brief is a conversation, written down and agreed by both sides.

blocks.text: Before the visit

items: Ask the client to send two or three photos of the room by WhatsApp, and any pictures of rooms they like.
Agree the visit time, and tell them you will need about an hour to talk, measure and photograph.
Bring your tape measure, notebook, brief form, phone with charged battery, paint colour card and a few fabric swatches.
For safety, tell someone where you are going and when you expect to finish, especially when visiting a new client alone.

blocks.text: The brief questions

head: Topic
Questions to ask
rows: What is the room used for? What should change about how it feels or works?
Who uses it, and when? Any children, older relatives, pets or special needs?
What do you dislike now? What is not working?
Which furniture, items or colours must stay? Anything sentimental?
Show me pictures you like. Which words describe the feel: calm, bright, traditional, modern, luxurious?
Favourite colours? Any colours you will not accept?
What total amount are you comfortable spending, including materials and labour?
When must it be finished? Any event, guests or move-in date?
Power supply, rented or owned (landlord permission for painting or drilling), access, parking, working hours allowed?

blocks.title: Ask about budget directly
blocks.text: Many people feel shy to name a budget. Offer ranges: 'Are we thinking under ₦100,000, ₦100,000 to ₦300,000, or more?' (illustrative). Without a budget, you cannot plan, and you risk designing something the client cannot afford.

blocks.title: From conversation to agreed brief
items: Listen and ask
Write the brief
Client reviews
Adjust and confirm
blocks.caption: Repeat until the client confirms the brief in writing, then quote.

blocks.text: From brief to concept

A **mood board** is a single page that shows the look you propose: the colour scheme, two or three fabric or finish samples, pictures of the furniture style and lighting, and the floor plan. You can make it with real samples glued onto card, or digitally in Canva or on Pinterest. Keep it simple and connected to the brief: each item should answer a line in the brief.

blocks.title: Worked example: a brief for a salon reception
blocks.context: For example, Grace owns a hair salon in Owerri. She asks Blessing to refresh the reception area, about 3.5 m by 3 m, before a reopening event in five weeks.
steps: Purpose: welcome clients, waiting area for up to 5 people, and show products for sale.
Problems: dark, cluttered counter, mismatched plastic chairs, no clear sign or focal point.
Must keep: the reception counter and the floor tiles (grey).
Style and colours: 'clean, feminine, modern'; likes blush pink and gold; dislikes red.
Budget: about ₦350,000 for materials and labour (illustrative); timeline: finished one week before the event.
Practical: building owner allows painting but no drilling into the front wall; work only on Mondays when the salon is closed.
Concept: soft blush walls with one deeper feature wall behind the counter as the focal point, gold-toned mirror, 4 matching chairs, product shelf with accent lighting.
blocks.result: A one-page brief that Grace confirms on WhatsApp, and a mood board where every item traces back to a line in the brief.

blocks.text: Listening well

Let the client talk first and take notes in their own words. When they use vague words such as 'modern', 'classy' or 'cosy', ask them to point to a picture, because those words mean different things to different people. Repeat back what you heard: 'So the main thing is more space for visitors and a brighter feel in the evening, is that right?' Notice what other household members say too; the person paying is not always the person using the room most.
Confirm in writing

After the visit, type the brief in short points and send it to the client: 'Please confirm this is correct, or tell me what to change.' Keep their reply. If the client later asks for something outside the brief, such as decorating a second room, treat it as a new item with its own price and timeline. This is called a **change request**, and handling it in writing keeps the relationship friendly.

blocks.title: Rented homes
blocks.text: If the client rents, check that the landlord allows painting, drilling or changing fittings. Suggest removable options such as freestanding shelves, curtain poles that use existing holes, or rugs and fabrics that can move with the tenant.

takeaways: The brief records purpose, users, problems, must-keep items, style, budget and timeline
Ask for a budget directly, using ranges if the client is shy
Every item on the mood board should trace back to a line in the brief
Get the brief confirmed in writing and treat new requests as change requests

activity.title: Run a practice brief
steps: Use the brief questions to interview a friend or family member about one room.
Measure and photograph the room.
Type the brief in short points and send it for confirmation.
Make a simple mood board with the colour scheme, two samples and the floor plan.
Record any changes the person asked for.
activity.evidence: The confirmed brief (screenshot of the confirmation) and a photo of your mood board

lessons.title: Pricing your work and writing a clear quotation
objectives: Compare fixed fee, day rate and percentage pricing
Calculate a quotation that covers materials, labour, transport, your fee and contingency
Write a professional quotation with validity date and payment terms
Present the quotation and handle questions confidently

blocks.text: A **quotation** is a written offer: what you will do, what it will cost and the terms. Once the client accepts it, it becomes the basis of your agreement. A clear quotation protects both sides and shows professionalism.

blocks.name: receipt
blocks.alt: A paper receipt with a total
blocks.caption: An itemised quotation shows the client exactly what each naira pays for.

blocks.text: Three ways to charge

head: Method
How it works
Good when
rows: One agreed fee for your design and coordination work
The scope is clear, such as one room
You charge for time spent: visits, shopping, supervision
Scope is uncertain or the client only wants advice
Your fee is a percentage of the materials and labour budget
Larger jobs where you manage all purchases

blocks.text: Many beginners start with a fixed fee per room, because clients find it easy to understand. Whichever you use, separate **your fee** from the **cost of materials and other trades**, so the client sees what they pay you for. Work out your minimum: what a day of your time must earn to cover transport, data, phone, tools and a fair income, then check that each quote pays at least that for the days the job takes.
What goes into a quotation

blocks.title: Building the quote total
items: Materials from your lists
Labour of other trades
Transport and delivery
Your design fee
Contingency, then total
blocks.caption: Add each part in turn so nothing is forgotten.

blocks.title: Worked example: quotation for a bedroom makeover
blocks.context: For example, Oluchi quotes a bedroom makeover in Benin City. All figures are illustrative; she uses real prices she collected that week.
steps: Materials: curtain fabric 8.1 m at ₦4,000 = ₦32,400; lining 8.1 m at ₦1,500 = ₦12,150; paint about 8 litres = ₦28,000; 3 warm LED bulbs and 1 lamp = ₦18,000; 4 ankara cushion covers = ₦12,000. Materials subtotal: ₦102,550.
Labour: painter 2 days = ₦30,000; curtain tailoring = ₦15,000; curtain track fitting = ₦8,000. Labour subtotal: ₦53,000.
Transport and delivery: ₦10,000.
Design and coordination fee (fixed): ₦60,000.
Contingency on materials and labour at 10%: 10% of ₦155,550 = ₦15,555, rounded to ₦15,600.
blocks.result: A quote of ₦241,150 in which the client can see materials, trades, transport, fee and contingency on separate lines.

blocks.text: Terms every quotation needs

items: Your name or business name, phone, and the client's name and date.
**Scope:** what is included and, just as important, what is not (for example, 'electrical work by client's electrician').
**Validity:** 'This quotation is valid for 14 days', because prices change.

**Payment terms:** for example, a deposit before you buy materials (many decorators ask for at least the full materials cost up front), and the balance on handover. Give the business bank account details, or a payment link through a service such as Paystack, Moniepoint or OPay if you use one.
**Timeline:** start date, expected finish date and what could delay it (fabric delivery, power, access).
**Changes:** extra work is quoted separately and approved in writing.
**Contingency:** how unused contingency is handled (returned or credited).

blocks.text: Common pricing mistakes

items: Forgetting your own transport for market trips and site visits, which can add up over a long job.
Quoting fabric without checking pattern repeat or width, then running short.
Not charging for the brief and design time when the client takes the plan and does the work alone. Consider a separate consultation fee that is credited if they go ahead with you.
Giving a single total with no breakdown, which invites suspicion and bargaining on every item.

blocks.title: Never fund a client's materials from your own pocket
blocks.text: Buying materials before receiving the deposit puts your money at risk if the client changes their mind. Wait for the deposit, confirm it in your bank app (not an SMS alert), then shop.
Presenting the quote

Send the quote as a neat PDF or image made in Canva, Google Docs or a free invoicing app, and offer to go through it on a call. If the total is above the client's budget, do not simply cut your fee. Offer options: a lower-cost fabric, a feature wall instead of four walls, or doing the work in phases, with curtains now and lighting next month. This keeps the quality of the design and respects their limit. Keep a copy of every quote you send, numbered in order (Q001, Q002 and so on), so you can find it quickly when the client replies weeks later.

blocks.title: Registering your business
blocks.text: As you grow, registering a business name with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) lets you open a business bank account and look more professional to corporate and shop clients. Check the CAC website for current requirements and fees.

takeaways: Separate your fee from materials and other trades on every quote
Total = materials + labour + transport + your fee + contingency
Include scope, exclusions, validity, payment terms, timeline and change rules
Offer options or phases instead of cutting your fee when a quote is over budget

activity.title: Write a full quotation
steps: Use your practice brief and budget table from earlier lessons.
Choose a pricing method and set your design fee.
List materials, labour and transport with real prices you collected.
Add 10% contingency and calculate the total.
Write the terms and produce the quotation as a one-page PDF or image.
activity.evidence: Your one-page quotation with all lines, totals and terms

lessons.title: Building your portfolio, getting clients and next steps
objectives: Assemble a portfolio from your projects with honest before and after evidence
Present your services and prices on WhatsApp Business and social media
Ask for testimonials and referrals ethically
Plan your next steps in skills and business growth

blocks.text: Clients hire decorators whose work they can see. Your portfolio, even with two or three projects, is your strongest sales tool. This lesson shows you how to build it, where to show it, and how to keep growing after this course.

blocks.name: portfolio
blocks.alt: A person presenting a portfolio of work
blocks.caption: Two or three well-documented projects are enough to start winning paid work.

blocks.text: What a strong portfolio contains

blocks.title: Portfolio building blocks
items: Testimonials and results
Project pages: brief to after
Before and after photo pairs
blocks.caption: Photos are the base; project stories and client words build trust on top.

items: **Three to six projects**, each with the brief in two lines, two or three before and after pairs, the colour scheme and why, and the budget level (for example, 'under ₦200,000').
**Range:** if you can, show different rooms or clients: a bedroom, a parlour, a shop, a short-let apartment.
**Process:** one floor plan or mood board shows clients you plan properly, not just style.
**Client words:** short testimonials with first names only and permission.
**Honesty:** only your own work. If you worked as part of a team, say what you did.

blocks.title: No paying clients yet?
blocks.text: Decorate your own room, a relative's parlour, a church office or a friend's shop at cost or for a small fee in exchange for photos and a testimonial. Document it properly; it counts.
Where to show your work

items: **WhatsApp Business:** set up a business profile with your services, area and hours, and use the catalogue to show packages such as 'Room refresh consultation' or 'Curtain and colour makeover'. Post before and after pairs on your Status.
**Instagram and Facebook:** post project carousels (before, plan, after), short videos of curtain hanging or styling, and tips such as the 60-30-10 rule.
**Google Drive or a PDF:** a 5 to 10 page portfolio PDF you can send to corporate clients.
**Offline:** a printed one-page leaflet or business card left with fabric sellers, furniture makers and estate agents who meet people furnishing new homes.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning one project into a week of posts
blocks.context: For example, Ruth has just finished a parlour makeover in Jos and has permission to post photos without faces or the address.
steps: Day 1: before and after pair of the main view, with one line on the main problem solved.
Day 2: the floor plan and how moving the sofa freed the walkway.
Day 3: the colour scheme with the adire fabric that inspired it, and the 60-30-10 split.
Day 4: a 30-second video of the curtains being opened, showing fullness and level hems.
Day 5: the client's testimonial with her first name and a 'Message me to book a consultation' line.
blocks.result: Five useful posts from one job, each teaching something, which builds trust and brings enquiries without paid adverts.

blocks.text: Testimonials and referrals

Ask for a testimonial when the client is happy, usually in your two-week feedback message. Make it easy: 'Could you write two or three sentences about what changed in your room?' Ask permission to use their first name. Never write reviews yourself or post fake ones, because one discovered fake can destroy trust. For referrals, simply ask: 'If you know someone who wants a room refreshed, I would be grateful if you shared my number.'
Packaging your services

head: Package
What the client gets
Who it suits
rows: One visit, brief, colour scheme and a written list of changes
Clients who want to do the work themselves
Brief, plan, mood board, quotation, sourcing and installation for one room
Reception, shop or salon styling with signage and display lighting

blocks.text: Clear packages make it easier for people to say yes. Write what each includes, its starting price, and how long it usually takes. Update the starting prices as your records show what jobs really cost.
Next steps after this course

items: Complete the capstone project: one real room, documented from brief to handover with before and after evidence.
Build your supplier list: fabric sellers, tailors, painters, carpenters, weavers and electricians you trust.
Practise the calculations (scale, paint, fabric, quotations) on every room you enter until they become quick.
Learn a free design tool such as Canva for mood boards and quotations, or a floor plan app.
Deepen your skills in an area clients ask about most: soft furnishings, event and short-let styling, or upholstery.
Review your prices after every three jobs using your budget-versus-actual records.

blocks.title: Your certificate
blocks.text: When you pass the module quizzes and the final quiz and submit your capstone with the evidence checklist complete, you earn the WODDI Institute Certificate of Completion in Interior Decoration Basics. Add it to your portfolio and your WhatsApp Business profile.

takeaways: Three to six documented projects with before and after pairs make a strong start
Show process (plans and mood boards) as well as results
Use WhatsApp Business, social media and offline partners to find clients
Collect real testimonials with permission, never fake reviews

activity.title: Launch your portfolio
steps: Choose your best one to three projects from this course.
Make one project page each: brief, before and after pairs, plan, colour scheme, budget level.
Set up or update a WhatsApp Business profile with your services and area.
Plan five posts from one project using the worked example as a model.
Ask one past client or room owner for a short testimonial.
activity.evidence: Your portfolio PDF or folder and a screenshot of your business profile

quiz.q: A client says 'make it modern' but gives no budget. What should you do before quoting?
options: Assume a high budget to show your best work
Start buying materials to show commitment
Ask directly, offering ranges, and record the agreed budget in the brief
quiz.explain: Without a budget you cannot plan. Offering ranges makes it easier for shy clients to answer.

quiz.q: Halfway through, the client asks you to also decorate the hallway. How should you handle it?
options: Do it free to keep them happy
Treat it as a change request with its own price and timeline, agreed in writing
Add it quietly to the final bill
quiz.explain: Work outside the brief is a change request; agreeing it in writing keeps the relationship clear.

quiz.q: Materials ₦100,000, labour ₦50,000, transport ₦10,000, fee ₦60,000, and 10% contingency on materials and labour. What is the total?
Why should a quotation include a validity period, such as 14 days?
options: Prices of fabric and paint can change, so the quote cannot stay fixed forever
It makes the client pay faster by law
